question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 61-64: 'Now cheer up, sir abbot! ... answer your quarrel.']
answer:
Context: The shepherd has heard the three questions, and now he answers the abbot's despair.

Explanation: He tells the abbot to "cheer up" and reminds him of the proverb, "a fool he may learn a wise man wit" - a fool may teach a wise man something. Then he asks for the loan of the abbot's horse, servants and clothing, promising, "I'll ride to London to answer your quarrel" (that is, to answer the king's charge). The stanza is the moment the plot turns: the humble shepherd becomes the champion. His confidence contrasts with the abbot's despair and with the failure of the universities.
explanation: The shepherd offers to take the abbot's place and quotes the proverb that gives the poem its theme.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 65-68: 'Nay, frown not ... fair London town.']
answer:
Context: The abbot hesitates at the shepherd's offer, and the shepherd answers his doubt.

Explanation: "Nay, frown not" means 'do not look disapproving or worried'. The shepherd says, "I am like your lordship as ever may be" - he is as like the abbot in build and appearance as anyone could be - and asks only for the abbot's gown, promising that "none shall know us at fair London town". The plan depends on a physical resemblance and on the gown, which is exactly the kind of practical detail that makes the disguise convincing and the story amusing.
explanation: The shepherd explains how the disguise will work.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 69-72: 'Now horses and serving-men ... our father the Pope.']
answer:
Context: The abbot agrees to the plan and equips the shepherd for London.

Explanation: He gives him horses and servants, "sumptuous array most gallant and brave" (splendid, showy clothes), and "crozier and mitre, and rochet, and cope" - the staff, head-dress and robes of a high churchman - "fit to appear, 'fore our father the Pope", that is, grand enough to stand before the Pope himself. The list of vestments stresses the dignity of the disguise: the shepherd will not merely look like an abbot, he will look like a prince of the Church. The greater the disguise, the greater the comic effect when the 'abbot' turns out to be a shepherd.
explanation: The abbot dresses the shepherd in full episcopal splendour, heightening the comic contrast.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 73-76: 'Now welcome, sir abbot' ... saved shall be.']
answer:
Context: The disguised shepherd arrives at the court, and the king greets him.

Explanation: The king welcomes him as "sir abbot" and says it is well that he has come back "to keep thy day" - to keep the appointed day. He promises that if the three questions are answered, "Thy life and thy living both saved shall be". The king is pleased because he expects to win; the audience knows that the man before him is not the abbot at all. The line also repeats the stakes of the wager: life and property.
explanation: The king welcomes the disguised shepherd, unaware that the answers are already prepared.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 77-80: 'And first, when thou seest ... what I am worth.']
answer:
Context: The king restates the first question to the supposed abbot.

Explanation: He asks him to say, "to one penny", what the king is worth as he sits in his place with his crown on his head among his noble liegemen. The question is repeated almost word for word from line 28, and this repetition is a ballad technique that builds suspense before the answer. It also shows the king's vanity: he cannot resist displaying his crown and his nobles while asking to be priced.
explanation: The first riddle is repeated, and the answer is now imminent.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 81-84: 'For thirty pence our Saviour ... penny worse than He.']
answer:
Context: The disguised shepherd answers the king's first question.

Explanation: He says that "our Saviour was sold" for thirty pence, so the king's value must be twenty-nine pence - "one penny worse than He", that is, one penny less than Christ. The answer satisfies the letter of the demand to name a value to a penny, while quietly telling the king that he is worth less than Christ. It is witty, daring and morally pointed: it measures royal pomp against the highest possible standard. The king's good-humoured laugh shows that he appreciates the cleverness rather than taking offence.
explanation: The first answer uses a familiar piece of Bible knowledge to make a bold joke at the king's expense.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 85-88: The king he laughed ... whole world about.']
answer:
Context: The king reacts to the first answer and asks the second question.

Explanation: "The king he laughed, and swore by Saint Bittel" - he is amused, not angry - and admits, "I did not think I had been worth so little!". He then asks the second question: how soon may he ride the whole world about? The oath and the laugh make the king a comic figure as well as a tyrant; he enjoys a good answer even when it is against himself. The stanza keeps the ballad's light, festive tone while moving the contest forward.
explanation: The king's laughter marks the change from threat to game.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 89-92: 'You must rise with the sun ... you ride it about.']
answer:
Context: The disguised shepherd answers the second question.

Explanation: He tells the king to rise with the sun and ride with it "until the next morning he riseth again", and then, without any doubt, "in twenty-four hours you ride it about". The trick is that the sun appears to travel round the whole world in a day, so a rider who keeps pace with it would complete the circuit in the same time. The answer is literally true if the king rides with the sun rather than trying to overtake it, and it turns an impossible journey into a piece of common sense.
explanation: The second answer solves the riddle by identifying the king's ride with the sun's daily circuit.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 93-96: The king he laughed, and swore ... what I do think.']
answer:
Context: The king responds to the second answer and asks the third question.

Explanation: This time he "laughed, and swore by Saint John" and exclaims, "I did not think it could be done so soon!" He then challenges the supposed abbot not to "shrink" from the third question but to tell him "truly what I do think". The repeated formula - laugh, oath, exclamation, next question - gives the poem a pleasing pattern and shows the king warming to the contest. He still believes he cannot lose, because no one can know another man's thoughts.
explanation: The third and hardest question is put after the king's second laugh.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 97-100: 'Yes, that shall I do ... pardon for him and for me.']
answer:
Context: The disguised shepherd answers the third question.

Explanation: "Yes, that shall I do, and make your grace merry" - he promises both an answer and amusement. Then he says: "You think I'm the abbot of Canterbury; / But I'm his poor shepherd, as plain you may see." This is literally what the king is thinking, so the riddle is solved and the disguise is thrown off in the same sentence. He adds that he has come "to beg pardon for him and for me". The answer is bold, honest and perfectly judged: it admits the trick, asks for mercy and makes the king laugh again.
explanation: The third answer is both the solution of the riddle and the unmasking.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 101-104: The king he laughed ... write nor read."]
answer:
Context: The king reacts to the unmasking and makes the shepherd an offer.

Explanation: The king "laughed, and swore by the mass" and declares, "I'll make thee lord abbot this day in his place!". The shepherd declines at once: "Now nay, my liege, be not in such speed, / For alack! I can neither write nor read." "Be not in such speed" means 'do not be in such a hurry'. His honesty is as impressive as his wit: he knows that an abbot must be literate and that he is not, so he will not accept a dignity he cannot fulfil. The refusal turns a clever trickster into a genuinely wise man.
explanation: The shepherd's refusal shows honesty and self-knowledge, completing the poem's praise of humble wisdom.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows after you have completed. [Line No. 105-108: 'Four nobles a week ... from good King John.']
answer:
Context: The ballad reaches its happy ending.

Explanation: The king grants the shepherd "four nobles a week" - a comfortable pension - "for this merry jest", and tells him to carry a message home: he has brought the old abbot "a pardon from good King John". The pardon cancels the death sentence and the forfeiture of lands, so both men are saved. The closing couplet resolves the plot neatly: the king's tyranny gives way to generosity, the abbot keeps his life and living, and the shepherd is rewarded for wisdom and honesty. The story ends, as ballads often do, with justice and laughter together.
explanation: The final stanza resolves the plot with a pardon and a reward.

question: Read the words given in the diagram and guess the theme of the poem. (Words: Discipline, Compassionate, Patient, Resilient, Courageous, Flexible, Honest, Humble, Conscientious, Persistent)
answer: All the words in the diagram name qualities of character rather than things: discipline, compassion, patience, resilience, courage, flexibility, honesty, humility, conscientiousness and persistence. Put together, they describe a person who controls himself, endures hardship without giving up, treats others kindly and keeps faith with what he believes. Since the poem is about Khahoris - wandering ascetics who give up comfort to search for spiritual truth - the theme is likely to be the moral and spiritual qualities required of a true seeker: self-discipline, patience, courage, humility and perseverance on the path to God. The words 'resilient' and 'persistent' in particular suggest a long, hard struggle rather than an easy journey.
explanation: Prediction task based on the word diagram; the guessed theme is confirmed by the poem's account of the Khahoris' hardships (lines 4-14).

question: Write the theme in the centre of the diagram.
answer:
Centre of the diagram: 'The qualities of the true seeker - discipline, patience, courage, humility and perseverance in the search for spiritual reality.'

In a sentence: the poem is about the inner and outer struggle of the Khahoris, who renounce the world and endure hardship in order to find God, and about the qualities that make such a search possible.
explanation: Open-ended diagram task. The centre statement is a one-sentence theme that covers all ten words and the poem's subject.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 1: traversed]
answer: "Traversed" means travelled across or passed over a region. In the poem the Khahoris "traversed that land, where even the knowing ones are lost" (line 8), so the word describes their long journey on foot across a desolate, trackless country. It suggests deliberate, patient crossing rather than aimless wandering.
explanation: Contextual support: line 8. Note that not every word in this list appears in the printed seventeen-line selection; the contextual meaning is drawn from the poem's account of the Khahoris' journey.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 2: ascetics]
answer: "Ascetics" are people who give up bodily comforts and worldly pleasures and practise strict self-discipline in order to grow spiritually. In the poem they are the Khahoris themselves - the wandering faqirs who leave home early, live among rocks and wear out their bodies in search of God. The line "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11) makes the word almost a definition of the only people fit for the spiritual life.
explanation: Contextual support: lines 4-6 and line 11, where the ascetics are the only ones able to light the fire.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 3: ridge]
answer: "Ridge" means a narrow raised line of high ground, especially the top edge of a mountain or hill. In the context of the poem it would be the rocky crests over which the Khahoris climb - the high, bare ground where they search and suffer. The word belongs to the landscape of hardship that the poem describes rather than to its printed lines.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; the meaning is given from the dictionary and from the mountain setting of lines 4-9.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 4: desolation]
answer: "Desolation" means a state of emptiness, barrenness and ruin - a place where nothing lives and nothing grows, and the loneliness that such a place brings. In the poem it fits the country the Khahoris cross: rocks, jungle and "that far off land" where even the knowing lose their way, with no trace even of birds.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; it summarises the landscape of lines 7-11.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 5: grieving]
answer: "Grieving" means feeling deep sorrow, especially after a loss. In the spiritual context of Sur Khahori it describes the seeker's sorrow at being separated from the Beloved: the Khahori mourns not for worldly things but for the absence of God, and that grief is part of his devotion.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; the meaning is fixed by the Sufi idea of separation from the Beloved, which the opening line ("those, who have Beloved seen") introduces.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 6: highland]
answer: "Highland" means hilly or mountainous country, land high above the plains. In the poem it is the high, hard country of rocks and secret paths where the Khahoris wander, far from towns and fields; the word supports the idea that the search for reality takes place away from comfort and crowds.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; it names the terrain of lines 4-9.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 7: rambling]
answer: "Rambling" means wandering about without a fixed route or aim; it can also describe speech that goes on without order. In the poem the sense is the first: the Khahoris' movement looks like rambling to the world, but it is in fact a disciplined search, so the word carries an irony - what seems aimless is the most purposeful journey of all.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; its meaning contrasts the world's view of the Khahoris with the poem's view.

question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 8: flicker]
answer: "Flicker" means to burn or shine unsteadily, with a light that brightens and dims; as a noun it is such a wavering light. In the poem's imagery the fire lit in the wilderness flickers, and so does the lamp of faith in the seeker's heart - small and unsteady, yet enough to guide him through the dark.
explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; the fire imagery is supplied by lines 10-11.

question: Read the poem again and encircle the correct option. 1. Khahoris trouble their bodies to attain their________.
answer: The correct option is (a) goal.
explanation: Line 6: "Giving much trouble to their bodies, they sought their goal." The poem's word is 'goal', meaning the spiritual aim of their search.

question: 2. Khahoris face severe________ while achieving their goals.
optionsRaw: (a) criticism   (b) conditions   (c) hardships   (d) all of them
answer: The correct option is (c) hardships.
explanation: Lines 4-9 describe bodily hardship: searching in the rocks, being "reduced to bones", dry faces and "slippers old and torn". They are not shown facing criticism, so 'all of them' is too wide; 'hardships' is the accurate summary.

question: 3. Khahoris never take their________ when they have goals.
answer: The correct option is (a) property.
explanation: The poem says the Khahoris give up "both the worlds" (line 14) and travel with nothing; they do not carry property with them when they set out towards their goal. (The printed sentence is awkward; if it is read as 'never take care of themselves', option (b) could also be argued, but 'property' fits the poem's theme of renunciation best.)

question: 4. "Khahoris' faces are dry, on their feet are slippers old and torn" shows the________.
answer: The correct option is (c) hardships.
explanation: The line (line 7) is a list of physical signs of hardship - dry faces and worn-out slippers. 'Struggle' is close in meaning, but 'hardships' is the exact word for the conditions described, and it matches the wording of question 2.

question: 5. Khahoris recognition is like ________.
optionsRaw: (a) caravan in desert   (b) raft in ocean   (c) guide in mountains   (d) safety in jingle
answer: The correct option is (b) raft in ocean.
explanation: Line 3: "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world." The world is the ocean and the recognition of the Godly is the raft that keeps the seeker from drowning.

question: 6. Khahoris can be found even where there is no trace of:
answer: The correct option is (c) birds.
explanation: Line 10: "Where not a trace of birds is seen, fire is lit". The place is so desolate that not even a bird is to be seen, yet the ascetics are there.

question: 7. In fourth stanza, the word 'save' is used in sense of ________.
answer: The correct option is (d) except.
explanation: Line 11: "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" Here 'save' is a preposition meaning 'except': who except a group of ascetics can light that fire? It does not mean 'rescue' or 'preserve'.

question: 8. True seekers can only be known to those who are for ________.
optionsRaw: (a) jungle dwelling   (b) deserted abodes   (c) mountain peaks   (d) spiritual realm
answer: The correct option is (d) spiritual realm.
explanation: Lines 15-17: "True seekers still exist, / Known only to those who are for spiritual realms". The phrase is repeated from the poem, so 'spiritual realm' is the answer.

question: Work in pairs and read the above selection again. Comprehend it thoroughly and paraphrase it in simple words. After you have completed, share it with your partner.
answer:
Paraphrase:

Mother, I have seen those people who have had a vision of the Beloved. To understand them one must spend at least one night in the company of those who live with God. The recognition of such people becomes a raft that carries one across the ocean of this world.

The Khahoris set out early on their journey. They search among the rocks and are reduced to mere bones; they give their bodies a great deal of trouble in order to reach their goal. Their faces are dry and their slippers old and torn. They have crossed a land in which even the wisest lose their way, and their secret ones speak of the secrets of that distant land.

In a place where not even a bird can be seen, a fire is lit. Who but a group of ascetics could kindle it? Those who went into the jungle were not led astray; those who took the highway were ambushed; but those who gave up both this world and the next were saved from ignorance.

True seekers still exist. They are known only to those who belong to the spiritual world, and having found that world they have built their nests close to it.
explanation: Open-ended paraphrase task; the model follows the six stanzas line by line in plain modern prose.

question: Read the selection again and answer the following questions. 1. How is Khahori's character depicted by the poet?
answer: The Khahori is depicted as a wandering ascetic who has given up both worlds. He sets out early, searches among rocks, reduces his body "to bones", and wears slippers that are "old and torn"; his face is "dry" from hardship. He is patient, disciplined and fearless, travelling through a land "where even the knowing ones are lost". He is also secretive and inward - "Their secretive ones, talk secrets of that far off land" - and utterly devoted, since he troubles his body only to reach his "goal". The poet admires him: his "recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world", and he is one of the "true seekers" whose nests are built close to the spiritual realm.
explanation: Character sketch supported by lines 3-9 and 15-17.

question: 2. How do the Khahoris experience sleep?
answer: The poem does not describe a comfortable night's rest, because the Khahoris have renounced comfort. They spend their nights in the open or in caves, on rock and hard ground, after long hours of prayer and meditation; their bodies are "reduced to bones" and they give themselves "much trouble", so sleep is brief and austere rather than refreshing. The opening lines suggest the right way to know them: "One must stay a night with those who with God have been" (line 2) - a night in their company is itself a spiritual lesson. Their sleep, in short, is a form of discipline: little of it, taken in a hard place, and offered up as part of their search.
explanation: Inference question: the printed selection mentions the night spent with the Godly (line 2) and the mortification of the body (lines 5-7), but does not describe sleep directly.

question: 3. Where and why do Khahoris spend their days and nights?
answer: They spend their days and nights in wild, lonely places: among the rocks, on the highland ridges, in the jungle and in "that far off land" where even the knowing lose their way, where "not a trace of birds is seen". They go there because their goal is spiritual, not worldly. Solitude removes the distractions of the marketplace, family and reputation, and hardship trains the body to obey the soul. The poem also suggests that the way is dangerous - some who took the highway "were way-laid" - so the desert is safer for the seeker than the crowded road. They are not running away from life; they are looking for its reality.
explanation: Textual support: lines 4-14 (the places and the dangers) and line 6 (the goal).

question: 4. What does the poet want to say when he says "Where not a trace of birds is seen, fire is lit"?
answer: He means that in the most desolate place imaginable - so empty that not even a bird passes over it - the ascetics still light their fire. The fire is both literal, the small fire of wanderers in the cold, and symbolic: it is the fire of divine love, of remembrance and of spiritual vision. The line therefore says that God is found where the world is absent, and that the inner light burns brightest where there is nothing else to see. The rhetorical question that follows, "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?", adds that only those who have renounced everything are capable of such devotion.
explanation: Textual support: lines 10-11, where the literal fire carries a symbolic meaning.

question: 5. What reward does a Khahori get after his hard work?
answer: His reward is spiritual, not material. The poem says that the recognition of the Godly "becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" (line 3): it carries the seeker safely across the troubles of worldly existence. The true seekers "have found" the spiritual realm and "have built their nests close to them" (line 17), which suggests peace, belonging and nearness to God. They are also "known" to those who belong to that realm - the reward of being recognised by the spiritually wise. In Sufi terms, the Khahori's hard work ends in union with, or closeness to, the Beloved.
explanation: Textual support: lines 1-3 and 15-17.

question: 6. Sur Khahori is the narration of Khahoris' struggle. Elaborate.
answer: Yes, the selection is a record of struggle from beginning to end. It begins with the effort of understanding: one must stay a night with the Godly to recognise them. It then shows the physical struggle - the Khahoris set out early, search in rocks, reduce their bodies to bones, and walk until their faces are dry and their slippers old and torn. Next comes the struggle with the country itself: they cross a land where even the knowing are lost, a place without a trace of birds. The poem then names the dangers of different paths - the jungle did not mislead, the highway ambushed - and ends with the hardest struggle of all, giving up "both the worlds". The final lines show the result: the true seekers survive and build their nests near the spiritual realm. The whole poem is thus a narrative of trial, endurance and arrival.
explanation: Open-ended elaboration; the answer traces the stages of struggle through all six stanzas.

question: 7. Which poetic devices have been used in this poetry? Write with the examples.
answer: The selection uses several devices. Metaphor: "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" - the world is an ocean and spiritual recognition a raft. Symbolism: fire stands for divine love (line 10), the nest for the soul's settled home (line 17), and the ocean for worldly life. Rhetorical question: "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11). Apostrophe: the poem opens by addressing "Mother!" (line 1). Alliteration: "Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones" (line 5) and "slippers old and torn" (line 7). Contrast: the jungle and the highway, and "gave up both the worlds" (line 14). Repetition and anaphora: "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14), and the echo of "known" in lines 15-16. Imagery: visual details such as dry faces, torn slippers and bones; and hyperbole in "reduced to bones". The verse is unrhymed free verse with lines of uneven length, which suits its meditative, translated style.
explanation: Devices are quoted from the printed lines, with line numbers.

question: 8. How do you express your emotions on the struggle of your friend or a family member?
answer: When someone close to me is struggling, I try to do three things. First, I listen without hurrying to give advice; often the person needs to say the difficulty aloud more than he needs a solution. Second, I offer concrete help rather than vague sympathy - sharing the housework when my mother is unwell, sitting with a friend the night before his exam, or going with him to the doctor. Third, I remind him of what he has already survived, because a person in the middle of a struggle forgets his own strength. I also pray for him and, if he allows it, pray with him. What I try not to do is compare his struggle with mine or tell him that it will pass. The Khahoris' journey teaches me that struggle is easier when someone stays a night with you, which is exactly what line 2 of the poem recommends.
explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the model answer connects the answer to line 2 of the poem.

question: Work in groups of three. Compose your own poem on the theme of Search of Reality, using elements of poetry based on three stanzas. Each member of group should compose 1 stanza. Once your group has composed the poem, exchange it with other groups.
answer:
A model group poem (three stanzas, one by each member):

I left the market and the noise,
the counted coin, the guarded door;
I walked into the hills alone
to look for something more.

The rocks were sharp, the night was long,
my shoes were torn, my lamp burned low;
but something in the darkness sang
the way that I should go.

I did not find a throne of gold,
I found a fire that would not die -
and all the world I left behind
was smaller than the sky.

How the elements were used: the three quatrains rhyme abcb (door/more, low/go, die/sky) and keep a steady ballad rhythm. The "market" and the "guarded door" are symbols of worldly life, the hills and rocks are the hardships of the search, the lamp is faith and the fire is the divine presence; "something in the darkness sang" is personification, and "smaller than the sky" is a comparison that measures the world against spiritual reality. The stanzas follow the same three stages as Sur Khahori: leaving the world, enduring the way, and finding a reality that is not gold.
explanation: Open-ended creative task. The model supplies a complete poem and an explanation of its devices, images and structure.

question: Work individually and write the central idea of the lines of Sur Khahori in your notebook. Once you have completed, exchange your work with your class fellows.
answer: The central idea of this selection is that the search for spiritual reality demands total renunciation and patient endurance, and that such a search is rewarded by nearness to God. The Khahoris give up home, comfort and even the good opinion of the world; they cross rocks and deserts until their bodies are worn out, because their goal is not wealth but vision. The poem presents the world as a dangerous ocean through which the recognition of the Godly is the only raft, and it insists that the real seeker cannot be recognised by ordinary people: "True seekers still exist, / Known only to those who are for spiritual realms". In the end the seeker finds a place near the spiritual world and builds his "nest" there. The message for the reader is that reality is not found in the marketplace but in discipline, humility and the company of those who live with God.
explanation: Central idea supported by lines 1-3 (the raft), 4-9 (hardship), 12-14 (renunciation) and 15-17 (the reward).

question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [1. Poetic Diction]
answer: The diction is simple, grave and intensely devotional. The translator has avoided ornate English and kept the plain vocabulary of Sufi poetry: "Beloved", "recognition", "ascetics", "spiritual realms", "seeker". Concrete words - rocks, bones, slippers, fire, nest - carry the abstract meaning, so that a spiritual idea is always attached to something the reader can see. The opening apostrophe "Mother!" gives the verse the intimacy of a family conversation, while phrases such as "that far off land" and "their secretive ones" preserve the mystery of the original Sindhi. Repetition of "those who" and "known" creates a liturgical, chant-like effect, appropriate to poetry meant to be sung in the company of devotees. The diction therefore serves the subject: it is humble in vocabulary and elevated in feeling.
explanation: Diction analysed through concrete nouns, devotional vocabulary and repetition.

question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [2. Theme]
answer: The theme is the search for Reality - for God - through renunciation and endurance. Everything in the selection serves it: the Beloved seen by the few, the night spent with the Godly, the raft of recognition, the Khahoris' early departure, their broken bodies, the birdless waste where the fire is lit, the dangers of jungle and highway, the giving up of "both the worlds", and the final nest built near the spiritual realm. A related theme is the hiddenness of true wisdom: the real seekers are not advertised, and they are "known only to those who are for spiritual realms". A third is the contrast between the world's idea of a wasted life and the poem's idea of a life well spent: what looks like wandering is in fact the most purposeful journey a human being can make.
explanation: Theme traced through the six stanzas, with the contrast between worldly and spiritual values.

question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [3. Structure]
answer: The selection is a short free-verse poem of seventeen lines arranged in six stanzas of uneven length: three lines, three, three, two, three and three. There is no regular rhyme or metre, as is usual in translated Sindhi verse, but there is a clear structure of thought. Stanza 1 (lines 1-3) states the vision and the raft; stanzas 2-3 (lines 4-9) describe the Khahoris and their journey; stanza 4 (lines 10-11) presents the fire in the wilderness and the rhetorical question; stanza 5 (lines 12-14) draws the contrast between the three kinds of travellers; and stanza 6 (lines 15-17) concludes with the true seekers and their reward. The movement is thus from statement to description to paradox to conclusion, and the short fourth stanza, with its single question, acts as the turning point of the poem.
explanation: Structure described by stanza lengths and the progression of ideas.

question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [4. Language]
answer: The language is metaphorical, symbolic and quietly musical. The controlling metaphor is that of the world as an ocean and spiritual recognition as a raft (line 3). Fire, nest, rocks, slippers and bones are symbols as well as objects. The poet uses a rhetorical question - "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11) - to make the reader answer for himself, and repetition with variation - "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14) - to give the lines a chant-like force. Alliteration ("Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones") and long vowel sounds slow the verse down, matching the slow, hard journey described. The tone is reverent and compassionate rather than excited; the poet speaks of the Khahoris with admiration and of the reader with gentle instruction.
explanation: Language analysed through the central metaphor, symbolism, rhetoric, repetition and sound.

question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [5. Message]
answer: The message is that spiritual reality is found only by those who are willing to give up everything else, and that such a search, however hard, is worth making. The Khahoris endure hunger, cold, rocky paths and torn slippers, and they surrender "both the worlds", yet the poem does not present them as pitiable: their recognition is a raft, their struggle ends in nearness to God. To the ordinary reader the message is a challenge - to ask what he is living for, and whether he is brave enough to travel light. At the same time the poem teaches tolerance and humility: true seekers may be hidden among the poor and the unimpressive, and only those who are themselves spiritual can recognise them. The poem thus combines devotion with a quiet warning against judging by appearances.
explanation: Message drawn from the Khahoris' renunciation, their reward, and the hiddenness of true seekers.

question: Work individually and identify the poetic devices in the selection. Make a list of them and use them in your sentences. Share your work with your class fellows after you have completed.
answer:
List of devices, with the poem's example and a sentence of my own:

1. Metaphor - "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" (line 3). My sentence: In the examination hall, my elder brother's advice was a raft in the ocean of questions.

2. Symbolism - the fire (line 10), the nest (line 17), the ocean (line 3) and the rocks (line 5). My sentence: The little lamp on our table is a symbol of the hope that keeps our family together.

3. Rhetorical question - "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11). My sentence: Who but a mother can understand a child's silence?

4. Apostrophe - "Mother!" (line 1), where the poet addresses his mother directly. My sentence: O Pakistan, how patiently your people have waited for justice!

5. Alliteration - "Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones" (line 5); "slippers old and torn" (line 7). My sentence: The sad, silent seekers sat among the stones.

6. Contrast - the jungle that did not mislead and the highway that ambushed travellers (lines 12-13); "gave up both the worlds" (line 14). My sentence: The rich man slept uneasily while the poor labourer slept in peace.

7. Repetition / anaphora - "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14). My sentence: Those who work, those who wait and those who pray are all serving the country.

8. Imagery - dry faces, torn slippers, bones, a fire in a birdless waste. My sentence: After the flood we saw cracked walls, broken cots and a single smoking fire.

9. Hyperbole - "reduced to bones" (line 5). My sentence: I have told you a thousand times to carry an umbrella.

10. Enjambment and free verse - the sense runs on from line to line without a fixed rhyme, as in lines 1-3. My sentence (a short free-verse couplet): The road kept climbing / and the sky came closer.
explanation: Open-ended device-hunting task; every device is quoted from the printed lines and used in an original sentence.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 1-3: Mother! I saw those, ... raft in this ocean of the world.]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: These are the opening lines of the selection. The poet turns to his mother and tells her what he has seen and understood about the people who have known God.

Explanation: The exclamation "Mother!" gives the lines the intimacy of a son confiding in the person closest to him. The poet says he has seen those who have "Beloved seen" - the mystics who have had a vision of God. To understand such people, one must "stay a night" with those "who with God have been": their holiness is not learnt from books but absorbed by living in their company. Their "recognition" - the knowledge of God that they possess - "becomes a raft in this ocean of the world", carrying the seeker across the dangerous sea of worldly life. The metaphor makes the world vast and drowning, and makes spiritual knowledge the one thing that keeps a person afloat.
explanation: The opening stanza states the value of the company of the Godly and introduces the raft metaphor.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 4-6: Khahoris prepared ... they sought their goal.]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: Having spoken of those who have seen God, the poet now describes the Khahoris - the wandering ascetics who set out in search of Him.

Explanation: The Khahoris "prepared early to depart", which shows both discipline and eagerness: they do not delay once they have chosen the path. They are "searching in the rocks" and are "reduced to bones", so their bodies have been worn thin by fasting, walking and exposure. They give "much trouble to their bodies" - they treat the body as a servant of the soul, not its master - and all this is done because "they sought their goal". The stanza makes the search physical as well as spiritual: the reader sees the rocks, the thin bodies and the effort, and understands that the spiritual life described in the first stanza has a price.
explanation: The stanza describes the Khahoris' early departure and bodily hardship in pursuit of their goal.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 7-9: Their faces are dry ... secrets of that far off land.]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The poet continues his description of the Khahoris on their journey.

Explanation: "Their faces are dry" suggests sun, wind and fasting, and "slippers old and torn" shows how far they have walked and how little they own. They have "traversed that land, where even the knowing ones are lost" - a country so trackless that even the wise cannot find their way - and yet the Khahoris pass through it. Their "secretive ones" speak "secrets of that far off land", that is, the mysteries of the spiritual world they have reached. The phrase "far off" keeps that world distant and mysterious for the ordinary listener, while the torn slippers keep the journey firmly on the ground.
explanation: The stanza combines physical hardship with the mystery of the spiritual country the Khahoris know.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 10-11: Where not a trace ... ascetics can kindle it?]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The description of the desolate country reaches its height in these two lines.

Explanation: The place is so empty that "not a trace of birds is seen" - no living thing crosses it - and yet "fire is lit" there. The fire is literal, the small fire of wanderers in the cold, and symbolic, the fire of divine love and remembrance. The rhetorical question, "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?", answers itself: only those who have renounced the world have the purity and courage to light such a fire in such a place. Here "save" means 'except'. The couplet is the spiritual centre of the poem: where the world is completely absent, the presence of God becomes visible.
explanation: The couplet uses a rhetorical question and the symbol of fire to show that only renouncers can reach the divine.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 12-14: Those who went to jungle ... ignorance saved.]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The poet compares different kinds of travellers and their fates.

Explanation: "Those who went to jungle were not misled" - those who chose the hard, lonely way were kept on the right path. "Those on high way were way-laid" - those who chose the easy, crowded road were ambushed, whether by robbers or by worldly temptations. The third line gives the reason: "Those who gave up both the worlds, were from ignorance saved." The "two worlds" are this life and the next; the seeker who clings to neither is freed from ignorance. The three parallel clauses form a contrast: the difficult road saves, the easy road endangers, and total renunciation brings true knowledge. The paradox is deliberate - what the world calls loss is here called salvation.
explanation: The stanza contrasts the jungle, the highway and total renunciation, and states the paradox of salvation through loss.

question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 15-17: True seekers still ... nests close to them.]
answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: These are the closing lines of the selection, after the account of the Khahoris' hardships.

Explanation: The poet ends on a note of reassurance: "True seekers still exist." The Khahoris are not only figures of the past. But they are "known only to those who are for spiritual realms" - the worldly cannot recognize them, because recognition itself requires a spiritual eye. Having found the spiritual realm, "they have built their nests close to them": the image of the nest suggests rest after wandering, belonging, and a settled home in God. The closing lines thus complete the movement of the poem from the raft on the ocean, through the hard journey, to the nest at the end - and they invite the reader to become one of those who can recognize the true seekers.
explanation: The closing stanza affirms that true seekers still exist and describes their reward as a nest near the spiritual realm.
